catalog_citation: Watters, John Robert. 1981. A Phonology and Morphology of Ejagham, with notes on dialect variation. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. xviii+549 pp. (SIL archive entry 9481)
catalog_locator: Part I, ch. 2 'Phonological Units', sec. 2.3 'The suprasegmental: tone and its phonotactics', p. 50
catalog_quote: 2.3 The suprasegmental: tone and its phonotactics The significant suprasegmental in Ejagham is tone (or pitch). Length does not have a significant lexical function in WE. In the Eyumojok-Ndebaya sub-dialect and other sub-dialects of WE, long vowels do occur in imperative forms of certain -CV verb roots, but these may be analyzed as two vowels separated by a morpheme boundary. ... Neither stress nor intonation have a significant function in the language in distinguishing syntactic or semantic categories. A given utterance can be described simply in terms of the interaction of the various lexical tones found in the given utterance and certain processes of tonal assimilation, deletion and downdrift.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ejagham is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Bendor-Samuel 1966 'Grammatical prosodies??' (Appendix IV of Pike ed., Tagmemic and matrix linguistics applied to selected African languages, pp. 192-196; Glottolog 70818), was already held by the project in the ERIC ED010547 full text and was read in full: it is a theoretical note on Firthian-style 'grammatical prosodies' (noun-class concord in Etung, subordinating particles and final low tone in Bimoba, English 'and') and says nothing about word stress; its Glottolog 'Suprasegmentals' tag is misleading. The only stress passages in that volume (pp. 257, 276) belong to Appendix IX on Legbo, not Etung. Nothing new was downloaded; the best first-hand stress statement for the language remains Watters 1981 p. 50 (p. 69, page scan verified this search of works with stress in the title): 'The significant suprasegmental in Ejagham is tone.. Neither stress nor intonation have a significant function in the language', i.e. a tone-only language with no functional word stress. one Glottolog download confirmed the bibliographic record (SIL bib 10241, language code etu). Records appended to Nothing remains to acquire.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ejagham is a tone language (three surface level tones plus contours, lexical and grammatical tone); the author states that stress (and intonation) has no significant/distinctive function, and gives no rule for stress placement -- prosody is described entirely in terms of lexical tone and tonal processes (assimilation, deletion, downdrift).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Vowel length noted as non-lexical in WE; surface long vowels in some imperatives analysed as V+V across a morpheme boundary.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language/utterance generally, not a word-level placement rule; sections 2.3.1-2.3.2 (pp. 51ff.) go on to describe lexical and grammatical tone, three level and three contour surface tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Watters 1981 describes the northern sub-dialect of Western Ejagham (WE, the 'Etung' area), based on the speech of the villages Eyumojok and Ndebaya, Manyu Division, Cameroon (ch.1 pp.15-16), with comparative notes on Eastern Ejagham (Keaka/Obang) and other sub-dialects. Same language as Glottolog ejag1239 'Ejagham' (ISO etu); older literature calls it Etung or Ekoi.

new_statements.quote: Borrowing from English to Ejagham is a process that is done from a stress-timed language,4 to a tone language.5 In such circumstances, loanwords from English into Ejagham are made to bear tones and function under the same tone rules as indigenous words of Ejagham. This phenomenon is made possible in that, speakers tend to match stressed syllables in English with high tones, and unstressed syllables with low tones in a spontaneous manner as evidenced below. [...] In the borrowed forms, the diacritic / ' / stands for stress. [fn. 5:] A tone language is a language having lexically significant, contrastive but relative pitch on each syllable (Pike 1948.3)

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Watters 1981 statement: Ejagham is a tone language in which stress is not a native category; the only mention of stress is as an English feature that is converted to tone in loanwords. It adds the loanword-adaptation detail (stressed syllable -> H, unstressed -> L) but no Ejagham stress rule. Different dialect basis from Watters 1981: this thesis describes Eastern Ejagham (Obang area, Eyumojock sub-division, p. 8), whereas Watters 1981 is Western Ejagham (Eyumojok/Ndebaya). The 2019 IJLC article by the same author already held by the project does not contain the 'Tones and stress' passage.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ejagham is a tone language, opposed explicitly to stress-timed English; stress is treated as a property of the English source words only, and in borrowing English stressed syllables are mapped to high tone and unstressed syllables to low tone (e.g. 'ma:stə > másà 'master', mi'kænik > màkánìk 'mechanic', 'ʃugə > súkà 'sugar'). No stress placement rule for Ejagham words is given, and the diacritic for stress is used only on the English forms.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 3.4.2 (p. 48): 'Loanwords do not have a fixed tone pattern' -- the stress-to-H mapping is a tendency; disyllabic loan roots show LH, HL, HH and HHL patterns (p. 49), and loans from Duala, Efik and Pidgin are listed alongside English ones.
new_statements.identity_note: Bakume Nkongho Ojong 2002 describes Eastern Ejagham (the 'Obang' area speech of Eyumojock sub-division, Cameroon; p. 8), while the catalog's Watters 1981 statement rests on the northern sub-dialect of Western Ejagham (Eyumojok and Ndebaya villages). Nkongho 2025 is by the same native-speaker author and lists the three dialects (WE, SE, EE) without naming a basis dialect; it notes that partial stem reduplication occurs only in Eastern Ejagham. Watters 2001 is titled for the Etung (Western) variety. All are Ejagham proper (ejag1239).

sources.note: Snippet (web search result summary of the paper): a critical review of tone-marking strategies in African orthographies; its Etung/Ejagham case reports that the 1960s orthography (Edmondson 1969) did not write tone diacritics but encoded the grammatical (tonally distinguished) verb categories at the prefix-root juncture with punctuation: colon = perfect, space = perfective, apostrophe = hortative, hyphen = conditional, plain juxtaposition for nouns - i.e. evidence that Ejagham verb TAM contrasts are carried by grammatical tone heavy enough to need orthographic support.
